stem: A 3-month-old boy is brought to the office for follow-up due to a unilateral cleft lip and palate.  The patient has been doing well, feeding with specialized bottle nipples, and is gaining weight.  As part of his multidisciplinary care, the parents are told that he will need to be monitored for ear infections and hearing loss.  This is because the patient most likely has dysfunction of which of the following muscles?​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌
explanation:
This patient has a cleft lip and palate, which can lead to problems with feeding, speech, and orthognathic (jaw) development.  Children with cleft palate also often have recurrent acute otitis media and hearing loss due to eustachian tube dysfunction.

Normally, the eustachian tubes open to equalize pressure and drain middle ear fluid into the nasopharynx.  Opening occurs upon contraction of oropharyngeal muscles, specifically the tensor veli palatini and, to a lesser extent, the levator veli palatini.  The tensor veli palatini originates at the interior surface of the eustachian tube and inserts into the palatine aponeurosis (soft palate).  In patients with cleft palate, the insertion site is abnormal, resulting in ineffective eustachian tube opening and poor middle ear drainage.

Fluid in the middle ear substantially dampens the movement of the tympanic membrane and ossicles in response to sound waves, resulting in conductive hearing loss.  Retained middle ear fluid also provides a medium for bacterial growth, which increases the risk of recurrent ear infections.

(Choice A)  The lateral pterygoid muscles depress the mandible (ie, open the jaw).  They are not impacted in a cleft lip or palate.

(Choice B)  The orbicularis oris encircles the mouth, acting as a sphincter to close the mouth and pucker the lips.  In a cleft lip, the muscle does not form a complete circle and instead inserts into the base of the nose on either side of the cleft; however, it does not impact the function of the eustachian tube.

(Choice C)  The stapedius muscle stabilizes the stapes, similar to how the tensor tympani muscle stabilizes the malleus.  Contraction causes dampening of sound transmission in response to loud noises.  It does not open the eustachian tube.

(Choice D)  The superior pharyngeal constrictor forms portions of the oropharyngeal walls and contracts to propel food into the esophagus.  Together with the tensor and levator veli palatini, it also seals the nasal cavity during swallowing.  Although this muscle is also dysfunctional in patients with cleft palate, it is not involved in eustachian tube opening, and therefore its functioning does not contribute to ear infections or hearing loss.

Educational objective:Patients with cleft palate are at increased risk of recurrent ear infections and conductive hearing loss.  This loss occurs primarily due to dysfunction of the tensor veli palatini, a muscle that normally opens the eustachian tube and promotes middle ear fluid drainage.​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌
